2c-x.note: All three quotes are on the pages as given. FRANK: 'The 2C family of drugs are classed as psychedelics (hallucinogens) but they can also produce stimulant effects'; ADF, same section as anchor 2: 'The '2C' group of drugs are psychedelics but can also cause stimulant effects'. The line is close to that ADF sentence in build but shares no run longer than three words with either page, so I leave it. Someone who has only heard the name learns it is a group of psychedelics with stimulant effects; the line does not say where the drugs come from, and no checked passage says it (ADF only calls the group 'a general name for phenethylamines').

2c-x.line: People can feel alert and warm towards others, and notice colours, sounds and smells more than usual.
2c-x.note: Anchors confirmed and the content is supported, but the line is FRANK's wording joined together: 'feel awake, alert and affectionate' (five words in a row from its sentence) and 'aware of colours, sounds and smells' (six words in a row from its bullet). The corrected line says the same and no more in our own words; hedge kept ('can').

FRANK: 'normally sold as pills or powders, but this can vary'; ADF: '2C-B usually comes as a white powder or crystal and is sometimes pressed into a tablet similar to MDMA'. Nexus is in both lists of other names. Longest shared run is five words ('a white powder or crystal'), a plain list of forms.

benzodiazepines.line: Benzodiazepines, or benzos, are depressants: drugs that make the brain and body work more slowly.
benzodiazepines.note: All three anchors confirmed. The line repeats ADF's stock family sentence: twelve words in a row ('they slow down the messages travelling between the brain and the body'). The corrected line says what 'depressant' means in our own words, as FRANK ('slow the brain and body down') and EUDA ('depressants of the central nervous system') support it. The first line does tell a newcomer what the drug is.

ADF sentence in full: prescribed by doctors 'for short-term or intermittent use to relieve the symptoms of certain health conditions, including anxiety or panic disorders, insomnia, alcohol withdrawal, and epilepsy'. 'Lab-made' rests on EUDA's 'synthetic substances'. NIDA entry 'Benzodiazepines' on the A to Z page confirmed. Own words; longest shared run four words (a list of conditions). (NIDA 'Drugs A to Z' was read in part: the first 100,000 of its 121,670 characters, which held this entry.)

All four confirmed (ADF list stands under the sub-heading 'Effects', after the words 'Effects can include:'). The line is near ADF's family sentence 'Depressants can make people feel calm, relaxed and drowsy' (ADF's GHB page has the same sentence with 'a person'), but it is three plain effect words that the drug's own passages also give (ADF list: 'feeling calm', 'drowsiness, sleepiness'; FRANK: 'Sleepy, relaxed, calm'; EUDA: 'calm (anxiolysis), drowsiness and sleep'); longest shared run four words in a seven-word line. Left as ok; the editor may reorder the three words if the echo matters.

ADF: 'Benzos most commonly come as a round or oval shaped pill'; 'known by their chemical (generic) name (e.g. Diazepam) or their brand name (e.g. Valium®)'. FRANK and EUDA give tablets, capsules and injections. Own words.

cannabis.note: All six quotes found where stated (EUDA heading 'About cannabis', profile dated 08.05.2013; NIDA entry headed 'Cannabis'). The line says no more than they say and is in our own words. One word is not plain: 'psychoactive'. The same pages allow a plainer wording if the editor wants one (ADF, next sentence after anchor 1: 'It's the component in cannabis that makes you feel 'high''; NIDA: 'intoxicating—mind altering—effects'), for example 'the chemical behind most of its high is THC'. The first line says where cannabis comes from and what is in it; with line 1 a newcomer understands what it is. (NIDA 'Drugs A to Z' was read in part: the first 100,000 of its 121,670 characters, which held this entry.)

ADF list under 'Effects of cannabis (THC)' > 'Effects', after 'Effects can include:' has 'relaxation and euphoria', 'laughter and excitement', 'increased appetite', 'feeling tired or drowsy'. FRANK 'How you might feel': 'Stoned', happy, giggly and/or sleepy, confused, paranoid. Each of the five words in the line is supported; own words; hedged.

All six confirmed. ADF's list is introduced by 'The THC extracted from a cannabis plant can come in many different forms, including:'. FRANK sub-headings are 'Weed' and 'Hash/hashish'. EUDA 'Other names': herbal cannabis and resin 'formally known as marijuana and hashish (or just 'hash')'. Forms and names only; own words.

cannabis.line: Doctors prescribe medical cannabis to ease symptoms of conditions such as multiple sclerosis, epilepsy and some kinds of pain.
cannabis.note: All four anchors confirmed and the content is right. Wording only, a judgement call: the line is ADF's sentence cut short ('Medical cannabis is prescribed to relieve the symptoms of chronic or cancer-related pain, multiple sclerosis (MS), epilepsy, Tourette syndrome, and a range of other health conditions'): 13 of the line's 16 words are that sentence's words in its order, though no run is longer than four. The corrected line says the same and no more, and keeps ADF's 'to relieve the symptoms of' ('some kinds of pain' from ADF 'chronic or cancer-related pain' and EUDA 'certain types of pain'; 'conditions such as' from ADF 'a range of other health conditions'). Epilepsy rests on ADF alone. The EUDA sentence (2013 profile) is about herbal cannabis sold on prescription in the Netherlands; the FRANK sentence stands under 'The law' but the line states no law.

dxm.note: All three confirmed (NIDA page shows 'December 2017'; MedlinePlus 'Last Revised - 01/15/2022'). ADF and NIDA give almost the same sentence ('is a cough suppressant found in many over the counter cold medications' / '... OTC cold medicines'); the line keeps its build but puts each term in plain words (cough medicine, cold remedies, sold without a prescription), longest shared run four words, so I leave it. A newcomer understands what DXM is. The lines never use the family word: ADF says 'When taken in high doses, DXM acts as a dissociative' and lists DXM under 'Examples of dissociatives'; left out, rightly, because that sentence is tied to an amount.

dxm.line: As a medicine, it eases a cough by making the brain area that triggers coughing less active.
dxm.note: Both anchors confirmed and the content is right, but the line copies ten words in a row from MedlinePlus ('activity in the part of the brain that causes coughing'), a page whose medicine texts are licensed from a publisher. The corrected line says the same and no more in our own words.

ADF list under 'Effects of DXM' is introduced by 'Effects start within 30-60 minutes and last for around six hours, and may include:' and has the bullets 'euphoria' and 'increase in positive mood'; the page says it 'looks at the non-medical use of DXM'. NIDA sub-heading 'DXM': 'Short-term effects of DXM misuse can range from mild stimulation to alcohol- or marijuana-like intoxication'. Hedge kept ('may'); no amount; own words.

ADF: 'It can also come in the form of cough syrup, gel capsules, lozenges, soft pastilles and pills'; other names 'DM, Robo, Robotripping, skittling, dex.' ADF Dissociatives page, heading 'Examples of dissociatives': 'It is sold in syrup, tablet, spray, and lozenge forms.' MedlinePlus sentence confirmed. Forms and names only.

ghb-gbl.note: All five confirmed (FRANK page heading 'GHB & GBL'; NIDA entry 'GHB'). Own words, longest shared run five words ('into GHB in the body', FRANK); the stock ADF sentence about messages is rightly not used. For a newcomer the first line works only if the word 'depressant' is already known: it is not explained in this drug's lines (line 1 gives 'relaxed, drowsy'). The sources would support a few plain words for it (FRANK: 'similar sedative and anaesthetic effects'; ADF: 'Depressants can make a person feel calm, relaxed and drowsy'), if the editor finds room within 20 words. (NIDA 'Drugs A to Z' was read in part: the first 100,000 of its 121,670 characters, which held this entry.)

ADF list (sub-heading 'Effects', after 'Effects can include:'): 'increased happiness and confidence', 'relaxation', 'drowsiness'. FRANK list after 'GHB and GBL can make you feel:': euphoric, drowsy, relaxed, turned on/sexy. All four words of the line are supported; own words; hedged.

ADF: 'GHB usually comes as a colourless, odourless, bitter or salty liquid, often sold in small bottles or vials'; other names begin 'G, fantasy, grievous bodily harm (GBH), juice, liquid ecstasy'. FRANK: sold as 'colourless oily liquids'; also called '1, 4-Bd, Gbh, Gbl, Geebs, Liquid Ecstasy'. Longest shared run five words ('usually comes as a colourless'), a plain statement of form.

FRANK (under 'What does it look like?'): 'GHB has a medical use in the treatment of narcolepsy'. NIDA: 'a depressant approved for use in the treatment of narcolepsy, a disorder that causes daytime "sleep attacks"'. Own words. 'Narcolepsy' is left unexplained; NIDA's words would support adding 'a sleep disorder'.

heroin.line: Heroin is an opioid: it is made from morphine, which the opium poppy produces.
heroin.note: All four anchors confirmed (EUDA heading 'About heroin', profile dated 08.05.2013; NIDA entry 'Heroin') and the content is right. Wording only, a judgement call: the line is FRANK's sentence with two phrases changed ('Heroin is a drug made from morphine, which is extracted from the opium poppy': 'a drug' became 'an opioid', 'is extracted' became 'comes'); 10 of its 13 words are FRANK's in FRANK's order, and 11 of 13 are NIDA's. The corrected line says the same and no more. Three publishers state this plain fact in nearly the same words, so some likeness cannot be avoided. The first line tells a newcomer what heroin is. (NIDA 'Drugs A to Z' was read in part: the first 100,000 of its 121,670 characters, which held this entry.)

ADF list (sub-heading 'Effects', after 'Effects can include:') has 'intense pleasure and pain relief' and 'relaxation and drowsiness'. FRANK 'How you might feel': 'Happy, relaxed, euphoric and/or sleepy, often in a 'rush' of effects.' EUDA: 'Apart from analgesia, diamorphine produces drowsiness, euphoria and a sense of detachment.' Every word of the line is supported; own words; hedged.

heroin.line: It is usually a powder, white or brown in colour, and is also called smack, gear or H.
heroin.note: All five confirmed and the content is supported. Wording only: the first half is FRANK's opening sentence with one word changed ('usually sold as a white or brown powder' became 'usually comes as a white or brown powder'), six words in a row. A marginal case (a plain description of form), fixed by turning the phrase round; names unchanged (smack, gear and H are in both lists of names).

Both EUDA sentences confirmed ('About heroin' and 'Medical use'). One publisher only, in a profile dated 08.05.2013. The source's word 'narcotic' is rightly not used. Own words; longest shared run three words.

lsd.line: LSD is a psychedelic made in labs from a chemical in ergot, a fungus found on rye.
lsd.note: All four anchors confirmed and the content is right. Wording only, a judgement call: the line is ADF's sentence lightly changed ('LSD is a synthetic chemical, made from a substance found in ergot, which is a fungus that infects rye (grain)'): 13 of the line's 17 words are that sentence's words in its order. The corrected line says the same and no more ('made in labs' from ADF 'synthetic' and NIDA 'lab-made (synthetic)'; 'found on rye' from NIDA 'fungi that grow on rye'). The first line tells a newcomer what LSD is.

ADF: 'is a psychedelic, which means it can affect all senses, impacting a person's thinking, sense of time and emotions'. FRANK: both sentences found under 'How does it make you feel?'. NIDA: 'can temporarily alter a person's mood, thoughts, and perceptions of reality'. Own words; hedged ('can').

All six confirmed. Anchor 0's sentence ('LSD stands for its chemical name, lysergic acid diethylamide, and is commonly called acid') does stand under FRANK's heading 'How do people take it?'; only the name is taken from it, nothing on how to take the drug. FRANK: 'usually sold as small squares of paper with pictures on them, known as tabs or blotters'; ADF: 'pieces of blotting paper (known as tabs)'. Form and names only; own words.

The three quotes are one ADF sentence, found under 'Long-term effects' > 'LSD and Mental Health': 'However, research into the administration of LSD in a safe, therapeutic setting, involving a controlled dose, has shown positive results in treating depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and reducing anxiety in patients with a life-threatening disease.' The anchors are confirmed and the line says no more than that sentence. I drop it because it is not an identity line: the brief allows a medicine line 'only if the sources say' the drug is also a medicine, and no page says that of LSD; this line reports treatment research instead, which on this site belongs to the graded answers (I did not open them). It also rests on one publisher's one-sentence summary, which follows a sentence about LSD worsening some mental health conditions, and it is that sentence cut short (16 of its 19 words are ADF's, in ADF's order) without naming LSD. The first reader's gaps note raises the same doubt. If the editor keeps it, a wording of our own that says the same: 'Studies giving LSD in safe therapy settings report good results for depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and anxiety in life-threatening illness.' NIDA's page (read for other anchors) is more careful: researchers 'are also studying whether some of these substances may be effective treatments'.

mescaline.note: All five confirmed. The ADF sentence about the two cacti does stand under 'What does mescaline look like?' (ADF's 'What is mescaline?' says only 'Mescaline is a psychedelic drug which means it can affect all the senses...'). NIDA entry under 'Psychedelic Drugs': 'Mescaline can also be lab-made (synthetic).' Own words; longest shared run four words ('can also be lab-made'). The first line tells a newcomer what mescaline is and where it comes from.

ADF list is introduced by 'Mescaline affects everyone differently, but effects may include:' and has 'euphoria' and 'perceptual distortions, such as bright lights or geometric patterns'. FRANK bullets under 'How does it make you feel?': 'An altered state of consciousness – with altered thinking and changes in time and perception' and 'Prominent changes in visual perceptions with intense visual distortions'. Own words; hedges kept ('can', 'may').

mescaline.line: It can come as a powder, a liquid, tablets or capsules, and is also known as peyote, buttons or mesc.
mescaline.note: All three confirmed (ADF spells the last name 'peyoto'; 'Peyote' is in FRANK's list). Wording only: the first half is ADF's whole sentence with one word changed ('Mescaline can be a powder, tablet, capsule or liquid'), eight words in a row. It is a bare list of forms, so the corrected line can only reorder it; names unchanged.

mescaline.line: Its use is thousands of years old, and it is part of some Native American religious ceremonies in Mexico.
mescaline.note: Both quotes are one FRANK sentence under 'How do people take it?': 'Mescaline has been used for thousands of years and is best known as a drug used by some Native Americans in Mexico as part of their religious ceremonies.' Content right and it is an identity line (what people take it for), with nothing on how to take it. Wording only: eight words in a row ('has been used for thousands of years, and') and then 'some Native Americans in Mexico'; 15 of the line's 19 words are FRANK's in FRANK's order. The corrected line says the same and no more. One publisher only.

methadone-buprenorphine.note: All five confirmed. NIDA says the same of methadone in the section before ('Methadone is an opioid medication that has been used for more than 50 years to treat opioid use disorder'). ADF: methadone 'as a treatment for people with dependence on opioids such as heroin or fentanyl'; buprenorphine 'in the treatment of heroin and other opioid dependence'. Own words; longest shared run four words. The first line tells a newcomer what the two medicines are.

All five confirmed. Two remarks, neither enough for a fix. Hedge: NIDA says buprenorphine 'can reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms', the line says 'reduce'; NIDA and ADF state it flatly for methadone ('while reducing their withdrawal symptoms and drug cravings'; 'It reduces the reward effects and cravings'), and NIDA's 'can' reads as ability ('Like methadone ... without producing intense feelings of pleasure'). Wording: the line joins two five-word runs from two pages ('reduce cravings and withdrawal symptoms', NIDA; 'people who are dependent on', ADF buprenorphine); both are the standard terms, and no single sentence gives more than 8 of the line's 13 words.

methadone-buprenorphine.line: Both can also be prescribed to treat severe pain.
methadone-buprenorphine.note: All three confirmed (NIDA A to Z entry 'Methadone'; ADF buprenorphine list after 'Buprenorphine pharmacotherapy can be used to:' ends 'treat severe pain.'). The line says more than they say for one of the two: long-lasting pain is anchored for methadone only (NIDA 'severe and persistent pain', ADF 'chronic or cancer-related pain'); for buprenorphine the only anchor says 'severe pain'. The corrected line keeps what is anchored for both. If the editor wants methadone's part kept: 'Both can also be prescribed for severe pain, and methadone for pain that lasts a long time.' The first reader's own gaps note says the same ('long-lasting' pain is said of methadone). (NIDA 'Drugs A to Z' was read in part: the first 100,000 of its 121,670 characters, which held this entry.)

ADF methadone: 'Methadone usually comes in syrup, injection, and tablet forms.' FRANK: 'usually a green liquid that is swallowed, but it can come in tablet or injectable form.' ADF buprenorphine, heading 'What does Buprenorphine look like?': 'Buprenorphine comes in three forms:' film, tablets, liquid; injection from 'Pharmaceutical names' (Buvidal, Sublocade) and NIDA ('extended-release injections, and implants'; implants are not in the line). The line lists forms only and compares no routes. Own words.

methamphetamine.note: All four confirmed (EUDA heading 'About Methamphetamine', profile dated 08.05.2013). The line joins NIDA's 'lab-made (synthetic) stimulant' and FRANK's 'Part of the amphetamine family of stimulant drugs' and leaves out NIDA's 'powerful' and 'with high addiction potential', rightly for an identity line. ADF's stock sentence about messages is not used. Longest shared run four words. A newcomer learns it is a man-made stimulant; 'stimulant' is not explained here, but line 1 gives what people feel.

ADF list (sub-heading 'Effects', after 'Effects can include:'): 'feeling euphoric and confident', 'talking more and feeling energetic'. NIDA 'Highlights': 'short-term effects typically include feelings of euphoria and increased alertness and energy'. FRANK list after 'Methamphetamine can reduce your appetite and make you feel:' begins exhilarated, alert, awake. Every word of the line is supported; own words; hedged.

methamphetamine.line: It comes as crystals, powder or tablets, and people often call the crystals crystal meth or ice.
methamphetamine.note: All five confirmed and the content is right. Wording only: the second half is FRANK's clause with one word left out ('the smokeable crystals are often called crystal meth or ice'), eight words in a row. The corrected line says the same; 'smokeable' stays out (a route).

EUDA 'Medical use' (2013 profile): 'Methamphetamine has occasional therapeutic use in the treatment of narcolepsy and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).' NIDA: the FDA 'has approved methamphetamine for treatment of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) as well as for short-term treatment of obesity'. 'Occasional' and narcolepsy rest on EUDA alone; ADHD on both. Own words.
